newsitem.title: USA: TWA's first quarter loss grows.
newsitem.headline: TWA's first quarter loss grows.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc. Monday reported a first-quarter loss, but said it finished the period "ahead of plan" and that some costs would decline in the second and third quarters.
Wall Street cheered the smaller-than-expected first-quarter loss, but analysts cautioned that a lean cash balance gave the carrier little room for error.

"First-quarter results reflect certain unusual costs -- including an accelerated narrow-body maintenance schedule and training costs associated with the phase-out of our larger wide-body aircraft -- that will decline as we move into the second and third quarters," said Chief Executive Gerald Gitner.

The airline said it lost $71.6 million, or $1.54 a share, for the quarter, beating analysts' expectations of a loss of $1.61 a share, according to First Call. A year earlier, TWA lost $37.1 million, or $1.46 a share.
Revenues fell to $762.3 million from $782.4 million.
The seventh-largest U.S. airline also said its cash position continued to decline.

St. Louis-based TWA had $136.5 million in cash and cash equivalents at the end of the first quarter, down from $181.6 million at the end of December. The company's cash balance has dropped more than half since the end of 1995.
"They need to build cash before next winter. The environment is strong, but I'm not sure they will be able to do that," said Glenn Engel, an analyst with Goldman Sachs.

Other analysts suggested TWA's cash balance did not give it much of a cushion to survive cyclical industry downturns. By contrast, Continental Airlines Inc., the nation's fifth-largest airline, ended the latest quarter with nearly $1 billion in cash on hand.
TWA had a difficult first quarter. Its auditors raised concerns about its ability to continue as "a going concern." The airline also was late in making some payments to some airports.

Those problems came on top of setbacks last year related to the crash of Flight 800 in July, the departure of former Chief Executive Jeffrey Erickson and a call by union machinists for the resignation of active CEO Gerald Gitner, who later became chairman.
Despite all that, TWA faces no immediate risk of bankrutpcy, analysts said.
In its earnings report, TWA said "the reduced revenue reflected a planned reduction in capacity resulting from the ongoing replacement of 747 and L1011 aircraft with smaller 767 and 757 aircraft.
"TWA also reduced the number of narrow-body aircraft in its schedule to move more aircraft through required scheduled maintenance prior to the peak travel season," TWA said.
Separately, TWA said it cut fares on round trip domestic flights from 11 U.S. and Canadian cities and on flights to five international cities from New York.
The lowest domestic fares are available Tuesday, Wednesday and Saturday and the domestic fare sale ends April 25.
The international fares are discounted up to 39 percent and that sale ends April 28, TWA said.
TWA said its operating expenses for the quarter climbed to $861.8 million from $836.6 million as the average cost per gallon of jet fuel rose to 74.02 cents from 66.58 a year ago.
TWA stock was up 18.75 cents to close at $6.81 on the American Stock Exchange.
